papers.title: Formation of Electron Velocity Distribution Functions at low-\{beta} Quasi-Perpendicular Shocks From Physical-Mass-Ratio PIC Simulations
papers.abstract: At low-\{beta} quasi-perpendicular shocks, the origins of upstream field-aligned electron beams and downstream flat-top distributions remain unresolved. Using 2D fully kinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations at the physical ion-to-electron mass ratio (mi/me = 1836), we found that the shock transition region is dominated by electromagnetic whistler-mode turbulence driven by the modified two-stream instability (MTSI) of reflected ions, not by the electrostatic instabilities as suggested by some previous studies using a reduced mass ratio. Beams in the upstream are produced mainly by shock-drift acceleration (SDA) at the ramp, whereas we attribute the downstream flat-top distributions to nonuniform acceleration by the parallel electric field. Electrons experience different field strengths, polarities, and interaction durations along their trajectories, leading to a spread of parallel velocity changes that broadens and flattens the distribution. These results highlight the importance of using the physical mass ratio in exploring the electron dynamics of low-\{beta} shocks.

papers.title: Funding Landscape of Early-Career Scientists: A Perspective from the AGU SPA Early Career Leadership Advisory Committee
papers.abstract: Like researchers across many scientific fields, early-career researchers in heliophysics face a critical transition from supervised research to independent scientific inquiry. However, the funding landscape that should support this transition is fragmented and unpredictable. Here we examine the current funding opportunities available to early-career researchers in heliophysics alongside the historical experiences of established scientists who navigated similar transitions. We catalog the major U.S. federal programs targeting early-career space physicists, documenting their eligibility constraints, selection rates, and accessibility. Access varies with career stage, appointment type, citizenship requirements, and solicitation schedules, and selection rates can swing sharply: the NASA Heliophysics Early Career Investigator Program (ECIP) selected 28% of proposals in 2022 but only 6% in 2024. To provide historical context, we collected survey responses from 30 researchers whose PhDs span 1972-2016 and conducted eight interviews with mid- and senior-career researchers. Most respondents viewed the present funding environment as more difficult than their own early careers, identifying predictability of opportunity, not ease, as what enabled earlier generations to build independence. Salary support alone does not guarantee opportunities to develop scientific leadership; accessible PI awards and real responsibility within collaborative projects can both contribute to that development. We recommend predictable, adequately sized grant programs for early-career principal investigators, transparent reporting of selection statistics across all early-career programs, continued use of dual-anonymous peer review, and named leadership roles for early-career researchers within large projects.

papers.title: The Role of Preceding CMEs and SIRs in Enhancing Shock Acceleration of Electrons
papers.abstract: The role of large-scale pre-existing interplanetary structures, including preceding coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and stream interaction regions (SIRs), in shaping the shock acceleration environment for energetic electrons remains not fully understood. In this study, we investigate nine interplanetary shocks observed by the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO) that are associated with significant MeV electron enhancements, as such enhancements are rarely observed at interplanetary shocks. We combine remote-sensing observations, drag-based modeling, and in-situ measurements to analyze the shock propagation through pre-existing interplanetary structures. Eight of the nine events are associated with a preceding slow or intermediate-speed CME, while six shocks are in-situ observed propagating within preceding ICMEs, indicating that large-scale upstream trapping structures are a common feature of these events. Further analysis identifies three distinct scenarios associated with enhanced electron acceleration: shocks propagating through preceding ICMEs, shock-SIR interactions, and direct injection of flare-accelerated electrons into SIRs. As a representative shock-in-ICME event, the 2012 January 29 low-$\beta$, quasi-perpendicular shock ($\theta_{Bn}\sim87^\circ$) is further investigated using observations together with one-dimensional Monte Carlo test-particle simulations of a shock propagating into a large-scale upstream magnetic loop. The simulation suggests that the upstream loop prolongs electron residence near the shock and substantially enhances acceleration efficiency. These results demonstrate that large-scale interplanetary structures can precondition the upstream magnetic environment, providing favorable conditions for prolonged electron residence and efficient shock acceleration.

papers.title: Scale-Dependent Statistics of Coherent Magnetic Structures in Early IMAP Observations
papers.abstract: We analyze early Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe (IMAP) magnetic field observations (November 2025 to May 2026) to quantify the statistical properties of helical magnetic structures and their relationship with turbulence intermittency. Intermittent structures, such as current sheets, are identified using the Partial Variance of Increments (PVI) method, and the scale-dependent normalized magnetic helicity is computed over scales corresponding to 0.5-3 correlation lengths. Prior studies have typically applied the PVI-helicity method to individual events; here we extend this technique to the ensemble statistics of a multi-month sample spanning many correlation times. To separate coherent helical structures from random turbulent fluctuations, significance thresholds for helicity are determined using phase-randomized surrogate realizations. We find a clear scale dependence in the occurrence, duration, and waiting time of coherent magnetic helicity, reminiscent of the scale-transfer arguments underlying inverse cascade, selective decay, and Taylor relaxation theories. Event duration and waiting-time distributions are well described by power-law and exponential models over different ranges, consistent with previous findings. In addition, PVI and magnetic helicity are anticorrelated, suggesting that high-PVI regions are preferentially associated with the boundaries of flux ropes, while their interiors tend to exhibit lower PVI and stronger magnetic helicity.
